power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 754 columns across 79 data files.
#### Issues Identified
6 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("WPPSI_reproducibility_2026-09-22.zip/WPPSI_reproducibility_2026-09-22/analysis/output/tables/Table1_observed_EGA.csv", "WPPSI_reproducibility_2026-09-22.zip/WPPSI_reproducibility_2026-09-22/analysis/output/tables/Table2_bootEGA.csv", "WPPSI_reproducibility_2026-09-22.zip/WPPSI_reproducibility_2026-09-22/analysis/output/tables/Table6_CFA.csv", "WPPSI_reproducibility_2026-09-22.zip/WPPSI_reproducibility_2026-09-22/supplement/frozen_tables/Table1_observed_EGA.csv", "WPPSI_reproducibility_2026-09-22.zip/WPPSI_reproducibility_2026-09-22/supplement/frozen_tables/Table2_bootEGA.csv", "WPPSI_reproducibility_2026-09-22.zip/WPPSI_reproducibility_2026-09-22/supplement/frozen_tables/Table6_CFA.csv" ), Column = c("warnings", "structural_consistency", "warnings", "warnings", "structural_consistency", "warnings"), Issues = c("⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 6 values are missing", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 83% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"0", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 6 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 6 values are missing", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 83% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"0", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 6 values are missing" )), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 79 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

info.title: The Cognitive Structure of the WPPSI-IV: What Can Network Analysis Tell Us?

text.text: The Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence, Fourth Edition (WPPSI-IV), is widely used to assess young children's cognitive abilities.
Its indices describe performance in domains such as verbal comprehension and working memory, but evidence for interpreting these as distinct abilities remains limited.

This study examined whether exploratory graph analysis (EGA), a network method, could recover the proposed index groupings from published normative correlations for ages 2:6 to 3:11 (n = 600) and 4:0 to 7:7 (n = 1,100).
Simulations tested whether the same method could recover those groupings when separate, correlated factors generated the data.
The main EGA procedure placed the primary subtests in one group.
It also produced one group in 99.6% to 100% of samples generated from the index models, so it could not distinguish those models from simpler alternatives.
In the older band, however, factor models fit better with several factors than with one.
Recovery depended on factor correlations, the number of subtests per factor, and a built-in check for a single dimension.
Groupings also changed with subtest coverage.
For school psychologists, a one-group network result, however consistent, cannot by itself show whether WPPSI-IV index scores reflect distinct abilities.
The Wechsler scales are among the most widely used cognitive assessments in school psychology, both in the United States and internationally (Benson et al., 2019; Oakland et al., 2016).
text.formatted: The Wechsler scales are among the most widely used cognitive assessments in school psychology, both in the United States and internationally <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Benson et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Oakland et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Interpreting patterns among their index scores is taught in cognitive assessment courses (Lockwood & Farmer, 2020; Miller et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Interpreting patterns among their index scores is taught in cognitive assessment courses <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Lockwood & Farmer, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Miller et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Widely used texts reinforce this practice.
The current edition of Sattler's assessment text connects intelligence theory with Wechsler interpretation and report writing (Sattler, 2024).
text.formatted: The current edition of Sattler's assessment text connects intelligence theory with Wechsler interpretation and report writing <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Sattler, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Other sources use cognitive and neuropsychological frameworks to link test results to explanations of a child's learning difficulties and to recommendations for diagnosis and intervention (Flanagan et al., 2022; Kaufman et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Other sources use cognitive and neuropsychological frameworks to link test results to explanations of a child's learning difficulties and to recommendations for diagnosis and intervention <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Flanagan et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Kaufman et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Within these frameworks, index scores become part of an account of how a child thinks and learns.

Proponents of patterns of strengths and weaknesses (PSW) methods use cognitive profiles to help identify learning disabilities (Schneider et al., 2024), and Wechsler profiles have been proposed as markers of ADHD and autism (see Wilson, 2024).
text.formatted: Proponents of patterns of strengths and weaknesses (PSW) methods use cognitive profiles to help identify learning disabilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Schneider et al., 2024)</ref>, and Wechsler profiles have been proposed as markers of ADHD and autism (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Wilson, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Several syntheses have not supported these diagnostic uses.
A systematic review concluded that PSW methods identify learning disabilities at the level of chance, regardless of method or instrument (Dombrowski, Benson, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: A systematic review concluded that PSW methods identify learning disabilities at the level of chance, regardless of method or instrument <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Dombrowski, Benson, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Across 19 meta-analyses, the estimated overlap between students with and without learning disabilities exceeded 50% on cognitive measures (Burns et al., 2025).

text.text: A meta-analysis of the WAIS-IV and WISC-V found that people with ADHD scored mostly at age-expected levels and that Wechsler profiles were not sensitive or specific enough for diagnosis (Wilson, 2024).

text.text: When a school psychologist describes an index difference as a distinct cognitive weakness, that interpretation can shape the explanation given to a family and the recommendations made to an educational team.
These uses also assume that each index measures a distinct ability.

The Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence, Fourth Edition (WPPSI-IV; Wechsler, 2012), reports three primary indices for children aged 2:6 to 3:11 and five for children aged 4:0 to 7:7, each based on two subtests.
text.formatted: The Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence, Fourth Edition (WPPSI-IV; <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Wechsler, 2012)</ref>, reports three primary indices for children aged 2:6 to 3:11 and five for children aged 4:0 to 7:7, each based on two subtests.

text.text: Interpreting one of these scores as a cognitive strength or weakness therefore treats performance on two tasks as evidence of a broader ability.
This study asks whether network analysis can distinguish the domains those indices are meant to measure.
Reviews of profile interpretation also point to a structural problem (Farmer et al., 2021; McGill et al., 2018; Watkins, 2000).
text.formatted: Reviews of profile interpretation also point to a structural problem <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Farmer et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">McGill et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Watkins, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Structural research addresses part of the problem by asking whether the proposed domains can be distinguished and how much reliable information their scores provide beyond general ability.
Because subtests share variance across domains, a domain score also reflects general ability (Brunner et al., 2012; Reise, 2012).
text.formatted: Because subtests share variance across domains, a domain score also reflects general ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Brunner et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Reise, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: A statistical model can separate domains even when their scores carry little reliable information unique to those domains (Gignac & Watkins, 2013; Rodriguez et al., 2016).
text.formatted: A statistical model can separate domains even when their scores carry little reliable information unique to those domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Gignac & Watkins, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Rodriguez et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: WPPSI-IV factor analyses have distinguished domains whose scores contain little reliable information of their own. Watkins and Beaujean (2014), analyzing the same published correlations used here, found that general ability accounted for most of the shared variation among subtests.

text.text: General-factor omega hierarchical was .78 in the younger band and .86 in the older band, and the older general factor accounted for 70.3% of common variance.

Specificfactor coefficients were .20 for Verbal Comprehension, .08 for Visual Spatial, and .09 for Working Memory in the younger model and ranged from .05 to .33 in the older model, including .11 for Working Memory and .05 for Fluid Reasoning.
These estimates describe modeled domain scores, including secondary subtests and two verbal specific factors in the older model.
They do not estimate the reliability of differences between published index scores.
Even the number of domains can depend on the models and subtests examined.

Studies of the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fifth Edition (WISC-V), challenged its five-groupfactor structure using the full U.S. standardization battery (Canivez et al., 2017 (Canivez et al., , 2018)).

text.text: Several normative studies reanalyzed the same sample, so their agreement reflects comparisons among methods rather than independent replications.
Other analyses support five domains. Dombrowski, McGill, et al. (2025) used Bayesian structural equation modeling of the 10 primary WISC-V subtests in 710 clinical cases.

text.text: Their five-domain model included a higher-order general factor and a residual association between Visual Spatial and Fluid Reasoning.
They reported simple structure and favored interpreting the indices beyond Full Scale IQ, while emphasizing general ability.
Exploratory analyses of the same subtest configuration in 5,359 clinical cases drawn from the same clinic supported four factors (Dombrowski et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Exploratory analyses of the same subtest configuration in 5,359 clinical cases drawn from the same clinic supported four factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Dombrowski et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The primary subtests have thus supported competing structural and interpretive conclusions across these studies.
Network analysis offers another way to evaluate the proposed groupings.
Exploratory graph analysis (EGA) identifies communities, or groups of connected subtests, within a network of their statistical associations (Golino & Epskamp, 2017).
text.formatted: Exploratory graph analysis (EGA) identifies communities, or groups of connected subtests, within a network of their statistical associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Golino & Epskamp, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In the networks used here, connections are partial correlations that account for the other included subtests (Epskamp & Fried, 2018).
text.formatted: In the networks used here, connections are partial correlations that account for the other included subtests <ref type="bibr">(Epskamp & Fried, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: A partition specifies which subtests belong to each community. Watkins et al. (2023) analyzed the 10 primary WISC-V subtests in 7,149 clinical cases with 10,000 bootstrap samples.

text.text: Their four-community solution combined visual-spatial and fluid-reasoning tasks, with 100% structural consistency for each community and 100% item stability.
These measures describe the stability of the observed solution.
Recovery addresses a different question: whether the procedure reproduces the structure used to generate simulated data (Christensen & Golino, 2021).
text.formatted: Recovery addresses a different question: whether the procedure reproduces the structure used to generate simulated data <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Christensen & Golino, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: A procedure can consistently combine subtests assigned to separate generating factors. Dombrowski et al. (2021) simulated data from normative correlations to compare rival factor models.

text.text: Generating data from each fitted model extends that approach by giving the procedure a known structure to recover.

Earlier EGA simulations examined two indicators per factor, but not at the factor correlations estimated for the WPPSI-IV. Golino et al. (2020) used 3, 4, or 8 indicators in their multidimensional conditions, with interfactor correlations through .70, and accuracy declined as correlations increased. Golino and Demetriou (2017) reanalyzed simulated data with 2 to 10 indicators for each of six factors correlated .70 (Keith et al., 2016) and recovered six factors regardless of the number of indicators.

text.text: Both studies assessed how many dimensions EGA returned rather than which subtests it grouped together, and both used earlier versions of the procedure.
The present controlled grid adds factor correlations of .80 and .90 and assesses exact recovery of each subtest's grouping under the current procedure.
It uses equal loadings and no cross-loadings, a simpler structure than the heterogeneous loadings and cross-loadings in the Golino et al. (2020) design.

text.text: Their study did not ask whether network communities reproduce the proposed index groupings, and their published matrices, derived from estimated networks, could not be reanalyzed here.

Subtest coverage also complicates interpretation of network findings. Lecerf et al. (2023) found three or four dimensions and substantial instability across five French WISC-V standardization age groups; final threedimensional solutions followed removal of unstable subtests. Dombrowski et al. (2026) found four communities in simulated data from the full 16-subtest U.S. WISC-V normative matrix.

text.text: Because these analyses used different sets of subtests, their results do not show how the smaller primary batteries are organized.
This study asked whether EGA could recover the WPPSI-IV primary-index groupings when those groupings were known to be present, and whether it could distinguish them from simpler structures.

It extends network research on the WISC-V (Dombrowski et al., 2026; Watkins et al., 2023) to the WPPSI-IV and pairs the network analysis with recovery simulations based on models fitted to the normative correlations.
text.formatted: It extends network research on the WISC-V <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Dombrowski et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Watkins et al., 2023)</ref> to the WPPSI-IV and pairs the network analysis with recovery simulations based on models fitted to the normative correlations.

text.text: Four research questions guided the analyses: 1.
What communities does EGA return for the WPPSI-IV subtests in each age band, and how stable are they across bootstrap samples?
Can EGA recover a known structure, including the WPPSI-IV index model, and under what measurement conditions does recovery succeed?
Are the communities similar across age bands when the subtests are held constant, and do they change when different subtests are analyzed within a band?
Do factor models fitted to the same normative correlations distinguish the index model from the merged and one-factor models?
Answering the third question required separating age from subtest coverage.
The full younger and older batteries differ in both.
Age-band analyses therefore used the seven shared subtests to hold the task set constant.
Paired simulations compared nested configurations within the same generated samples to isolate the effect of changing coverage.
Analyses used published correlations from the WPPSI-IV Technical and Interpretive Manual (Wechsler, 2012, Table  5.1).

The correlations were transcribed twice from photographs of the manual, with no discrepancies among the 126 distinct off-diagonal coefficients.
Both matrices were symmetric and positive definite.
Six subtest configurations were analyzed.
The younger-band full battery contains Information, Receptive Vocabulary, Picture Naming, Block Design, Object Assembly, Picture Memory, and Zoo Locations.
The younger-band primary subtests omit Picture Naming, leaving the three primary index pairs.
The older-band full battery contains all 15 older-band subtests.

The older-band primary subtests are Information and Similarities, Block Design and Object Assembly, Matrix Reasoning and Picture Concepts, Picture Memory and Zoo Locations, and Bug Search and Cancellation.
These pairs represent Verbal Comprehension, Visual Spatial, Fluid Reasoning, Working Memory, and Processing Speed, respectively.
The shared subtests are the seven subtests given in both age bands, analyzed in the same order in each band.
In the younger band, the shared subtests are identical to the full battery, so the six configurations represent five distinct matrices derived from two normative sources.
The full batteries describe the larger sets of subtests, the primary subtests address the index groupings, and the shared subtests permit age-band comparisons using matched tasks.
The main EGA procedure used the graphical least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (GLASSO) to estimate a Gaussian graphical model (Friedman et al., 2008).

Three models were fitted to each primary correlation matrix by maximum likelihood in lavaan, with standardized latent variables and no post hoc modification.

Each band also included a one-factor model.

text.text: With two indicators and ρ = .50, increasing λ from .60 to .80 raised recovery from .465 to .908.
Across the full design, recovery was lower with five factors than with three, .637 versus .798.
In the one-factor simulations, the main EGA procedure produced two false splits across 24,000 replicates, both at N = 300 with λ = .60 and at least 15 indicators.
Without the check, false splitting averaged .190 and declined from .305 at N = 300 to .112 at N = 2,000.
For 15 and 20 indicators, rates remained between .17 and .23 at N = 2,000, pooled across loadings.
For six indicators, no false split occurred in 1,500 usable replicates at that sample size.
No failures occurred with the check (0 of 24,000); the failure rate without the check was 0.36%.
The shared subtests were grouped identically in both age bands: one community with the check and the same verbal-nonverbal partition without it (ARI = 1.00; Table 3).
text.formatted: The shared subtests were grouped identically in both age bands: one community with the check and the same verbal-nonverbal partition without it (ARI = 1.00; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>).

text.text: Without the check, two communities recurred in 74.3% of younger-band and 99.8% of older-band bootstrap replicates.
In the paired simulations, the older-band full battery returned three communities in 87.1% of replicates.
Restricting the same samples to the primary subtests produced one community in 100% with the check.
Without it, the primary subset returned three communities in 50.7% and two in 44.8%, and matched the full-battery grouping only partly (mean ARI = .52).
Restricting to the seven shared subtests yielded one community in 100% with the check and two in 99.8% without it.
In the younger band, removing Picture Naming changed the result without the check from two communities in 77.8% of replicates to one in 53.8% and two in 45.3%.
All younger factor models had favorable approximate fit (Table 4).
text.formatted: All younger factor models had favorable approximate fit (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref>).

text.text: The index model yielded χ² = 2.9 with six degrees of freedom, CFI = 1.000, RMSEA = .000, and SRMR = .009.
Its factor correlations ranged from .84 to .85.
BIC values were 9412.5, 9406.5, and 9412.4 for the one-factor, merged, and index models, respectively.
In the older band, the one-factor model fit less well than either multifactor model.
CFI was .923, .980, and .991 for the one-factor, merged, and index models; corresponding RMSEA values were .085, .045, and .034.
The index model had better approximate fit.
BIC provided little separation between the merged and index models, 27867.3 versus 27868.7, respectively.
Older index-model factor correlations ranged from .60 to .87.
Visual Spatial correlated .87 with Fluid Reasoning and .81 with Working Memory, and Fluid Reasoning correlated .86 with Working Memory.
The main EGA procedure consistently grouped the WPPSI-IV primary subtests together, but the recovery simulations showed why that result did not settle their structure.
It returned a single community in 100% of younger-band samples and 99.6% of older-band samples generated from the index models, nearly matching its behavior under the merged and one-factor models.
A stable one-community result therefore provided little basis for choosing among these competing accounts of the primary indices.
Factor models fitted to the same correlations offered a separate comparison, and in the older band they fit better with several factors than with one.

The present study adds recovery simulations to the questions addressed by earlier WISC-V network studies. Watkins et al. (2023) found four highly stable communities among the 10 primary WISC-V subtests, with the visual-spatial and fluid-reasoning subtests combined.
text.formatted: The present study adds recovery simulations to the questions addressed by earlier WISC-V network studies. <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Watkins et al. (2023)</ref> found four highly stable communities among the 10 primary WISC-V subtests, with the visual-spatial and fluid-reasoning subtests combined.

text.text: They used GLASSO and Walktrap in EGAnet 1.2.3 and assessed how consistently subtests were assigned to communities. Dombrowski et al. (2026) found four communities in the full 16subtest WISC-V, combining Visual Spatial and Fluid Reasoning while keeping Working Memory separate, and assessed the stability of subtest strength centrality and the precision of network connections (Epskamp et al., 2018).
text.formatted: They used GLASSO and Walktrap in EGAnet 1.2.3 and assessed how consistently subtests were assigned to communities. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Dombrowski et al. (2026)</ref> found four communities in the full 16subtest WISC-V, combining Visual Spatial and Fluid Reasoning while keeping Working Memory separate, and assessed the stability of subtest strength centrality and the precision of network connections <ref type="bibr">(Epskamp et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: These analyses address how stable a network estimate is.
Recovery simulations address whether a procedure can distinguish the structures it is being used to evaluate.
The two questions can have different answers.

In the present study, the one-community solutions for the primary subtests recurred in 99.8% to 100% of bootstrap samples, yet the procedure returned one community in 99.6% to 100% of samples generated from the index models.
A highly stable solution therefore did not show that the index structure was absent.
Whether the same limits apply to the WISC-V would require WISC-V calibration.
The unidimensionality check helps explain why the procedure so often combined the subtests.
When the check finds a single community, that answer replaces the network's community solution.
In the controlled one-factor simulations, it nearly eliminated false splitting: 2 false splits occurred in 24,000 samples, compared with an average rate of .190 without the check.
Yet the same check suppressed distinctions specified in multidimensional generating models.
In the fitted-model simulations, dropping the check improved recovery of the broader merged groupings but still almost never recovered the indices themselves.
For the older-band primary subtests, the procedure without the check returned three communities, yet it recovered the index partition in 0 of 998 samples generated from the index model.
Several communities therefore did not mean the intended distinctions had been recovered.
Without the check, the procedure also split one-factor data in 4.3% of younger-band and 25.5% of older-band samples.
Recovery depended jointly on indicator count and factor correlations.
With two indicators, exact recovery under the main EGA procedure fell from .565 at a factor correlation of .50 to .001 at .70; no usable sample recovered the groupings at .80 or .90.
The fitted WPPSI-IV models contained similarly high correlations: .84 to .85 among the younger factors, and .81 to .87 among Visual Spatial, Fluid Reasoning, and Working Memory in the older band.
These conditions help explain the difficulty of recovery.

The grid's equal loadings and uniform correlations, however, do not reproduce the heterogeneous fitted models exactly. Golino and Demetriou (2017) recovered the number of factors with two indicators per factor correlated .70, whereas the main EGA procedure here almost never recovered even the number of factors under that condition.
text.formatted: The grid's equal loadings and uniform correlations, however, do not reproduce the heterogeneous fitted models exactly. <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Golino and Demetriou (2017)</ref> recovered the number of factors with two indicators per factor correlated .70, whereas the main EGA procedure here almost never recovered even the number of factors under that condition.

text.text: The two designs differed in the number of factors, loadings, and procedure version, and the present results do not show which difference accounts for the contrast.

Larger samples did not consistently improve recovery under the main EGA procedure; with two indicators per factor and a factor correlation of .60, its recovery fell from .088 at N = 300 to .002 at N = 2,000.
Without the check, larger samples improved recovery in some conditions.
The benefit of additional observations therefore depended on the procedure as well as the measurement conditions.
The paired comparisons showed directly why the task set matters.
The full older battery produced three communities in 87.1% of paired samples, while its 10 primary subtests produced one community every time with the check.

In the younger band, dropping Picture Naming shifted the result without the check from two communities in 77.8% of samples to a near-even split between one and two. Dombrowski et al. (2022) argued for examining the WISC-V primary battery separately, and McGrew et al. (2023) tested whether their network conclusions about Woodcock-Johnson IV domains held under different selections of measures.
text.formatted: In the younger band, dropping Picture Naming shifted the result without the check from two communities in 77.8% of samples to a near-even split between one and two. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Dombrowski et al. (2022)</ref> argued for examining the WISC-V primary battery separately, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">McGrew et al. (2023)</ref> tested whether their network conclusions about Woodcock-Johnson IV domains held under different selections of measures.

text.text: Here, comparisons within the same generated samples showed that full-battery findings did not automatically carry over to the primary indices.
A school psychologist reading a full-battery network study therefore cannot assume that its groupings describe the primary index scores reported for a child.
The same coverage issue affects comparisons between age bands.
Restricting both WPPSI-IV analyses to the same seven subtests produced identical groupings with different bootstrap stability.
Full-battery differences therefore cannot be attributed to age alone.
These comparisons did not test longitudinal change or measurement invariance across ages.
Factor models fitted to the same normative correlations did not support a one-factor account of the older-band primary subtests.
In the older band, both multifactor models fit better than a one-factor model (CFI .980 and .991 versus .923).
The index model had better approximate fit than the merged model, although BIC did not clearly separate them.
All three younger-band models fit well, although BIC favored the merged model.

The observed onecommunity solution did not establish a one-factor account of either age band. Dombrowski, McGill, et al. (2025) likewise found that a multidimensional model fit the WISC-V primary subtests and favored interpreting the indices beyond Full Scale IQ.
text.formatted: The observed onecommunity solution did not establish a one-factor account of either age band. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Dombrowski, McGill, et al. (2025)</ref> likewise found that a multidimensional model fit the WISC-V primary subtests and favored interpreting the indices beyond Full Scale IQ.

text.text: Model fit of this kind supports a structure; it does not establish the accuracy of an individual child's profile.
A child may perform relatively poorly on Picture Memory and Zoo Locations and also struggle to follow classroom instructions.
The WPPSI-IV Working Memory Index summarizes performance on those two test tasks (Wechsler, 2012).
text.formatted: The WPPSI-IV Working Memory Index summarizes performance on those two test tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Wechsler, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: A school psychologist who attributes the classroom difficulty to a working-memory weakness adds a causal explanation that the score alone cannot establish.

Across a broader executive-function literature, performance-based measures correlate weakly with ratings of everyday executive functioning (median r = .19; Toplak et al., 2013), and WAIS-IV and WISC-V profiles have not proved sensitive or specific enough to diagnose ADHD (Wilson, 2024).
text.formatted: Across a broader executive-function literature, performance-based measures correlate weakly with ratings of everyday executive functioning (median r = .19; <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Toplak et al., 2013)</ref>, and WAIS-IV and WISC-V profiles have not proved sensitive or specific enough to diagnose ADHD <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Wilson, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Reviews of profile interpretation have also questioned the educational usefulness of such inferences (Farmer et al., 2021; McGill et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Reviews of profile interpretation have also questioned the educational usefulness of such inferences <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Farmer et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">McGill et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Score reliability and the accuracy of profile differences pose separate problems for such interpretations. Watkins and Beaujean (2014) found little reliable variance specific to modeled WPPSI-IV domains after accounting for general ability; their coefficients do not directly assess index-score differences.
text.formatted: Score reliability and the accuracy of profile differences pose separate problems for such interpretations. <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Watkins and Beaujean (2014)</ref> found little reliable variance specific to modeled WPPSI-IV domains after accounting for general ability; their coefficients do not directly assess index-score differences.

text.text: De Jong (2023) examined discrepancies between index scores and overall performance in the Dutch WISC-V and found that only 40% to 74% were accompanied by a discrepancy on the corresponding broad factor.
Clinical guidance recommends considering scores alongside history, behavior, and other assessment information (Kaufman et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Clinical guidance recommends considering scores alongside history, behavior, and other assessment information <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Kaufman et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Agreement among sources does not establish a cognitive cause or show that a profile-based intervention will help (McGill et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Agreement among sources does not establish a cognitive cause or show that a profile-based intervention will help <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(McGill et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: A report can describe memory-task performance and classroom difficulty separately, then identify the evidence for any proposed connection.
Intervention recommendations require evidence of benefit for the observed difficulty, which neither factor-model fit nor network stability supplies.
The analyses used published, rounded correlations, so individual score distributions could not be examined.
Simulations assumed multivariate normality and held fitted values fixed.
Because the models were fitted to the same correlations being analyzed, recovery results depend on those approximations.
They neither incorporate parameter uncertainty nor independently confirm population structure.
The controlled simulation used equal loadings, uniform factor correlations, and no crossloadings.
The fitted WPPSI-IV models are less uniform.
Summary rates pool usable samples across conditions with different recovery rates and exclude samples in which the procedure failed to return a usable result.
The one-factor simulations were added after the main results had been analyzed and interpreted.
Recovery simulations compared the main EGA procedure with the version omitting its unidimensionality check.
Other estimation, community-detection, and factor-retention methods were not compared on those data.
Recovery was tested only for the primary subtests, leaving the full older battery's three-community result untested.
No independent clinical WPPSI-IV sample or measure of diagnostic accuracy, intervention benefit, or child functioning was analyzed.
The main EGA procedure grouped the WPPSI-IV primary subtests together, but it did the same when the simulated data contained separate correlated factors.
Its result therefore cannot show whether the indices capture distinct parts of a young child's developing cognitive abilities, and it changed when different subtests were analyzed.
In the older band, factor models fit better with several factors than with one, and the index model had better approximate fit than the merged model, but BIC barely separated the two.
In the younger band, all three factor models fit well, although BIC favored the merged model.
For school psychologists, a network finding like this one does not settle what an index score means.

That question depends on evidence about the scores themselves, such as how reliably index differences can be measured and whether they relate to a child's functioning, which this study did not examine.
